definition: The average absolute difference between predictions and targets — a robust regression metric less sensitive to outliers than squared error.
details: The average absolute difference between predictions and targets — a robust regression metric less sensitive to outliers than squared error.

explainer.lead: Mean absolute error scores a regression model by the average size of its misses, ignoring direction. It matters because it stays readable in the target's own units and is not dominated by a few extreme points.

tiers.eli5: If you guess people's ages and are off by 3, then 5, then 1 year, the score is the plain average of those misses: 3 years.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers report MAE when they want an error figure in the same units as the target and when outliers should not swamp the metric. A pitfall is that the absolute value is not differentiable at zero, which complicates gradient-based training.
tiers.paperLevel: MAE = (1/n) * sum over i of |y_i - yhat_i|. Because errors enter linearly rather than squared, large deviations count proportionally less than under squared error.

explainer.example: Predictions of 10, 20, 30 against targets of 12, 18, 33 give absolute errors 2, 2, 3, averaging to an MAE of 2.33.
